title: Joined Starbucks as director of retail operations and marketing
statement: After noticing unusually large filter orders from a small Seattle coffee retailer while running Hammarplast's U.S. operations, Schultz visited the store in 1981 and joined Starbucks a year later at age twenty-nine as director of retail operations and marketing.
outcome: Within five years he had left to found Il Giornale and returned to acquire the entire company, converting a six-store bean retailer into the platform for a national espresso-bar chain.

title: Founded Il Giornale after the espresso-bar pilot was rejected
statement: After owners Jerry Baldwin and Gordon Bowker declined to roll out the café concept beyond a successful 1984 pilot, Schultz left Starbucks and raised roughly $400,000, surviving rejection from 217 of 242 investors, to open Il Giornale, an Italian-style espresso bar named after a Milanese newspaper.
outcome: With Starbucks as first investor and chief coffee buyer Dave Olsen as partner, Il Giornale opened three Seattle locations before the 1987 acquisition opportunity arrived.

title: Acquired Starbucks' retail unit and merged it into Il Giornale
statement: When the original owners decided to focus on Peet's, Schultz raised $3.8 million by August 1987 to buy the Starbucks name, roasting plant, and six Seattle stores, rebranding his Il Giornale outlets under the Starbucks name.
outcome: The combined company opened its first stores outside Seattle, in Vancouver and Chicago, the same year, reached 46 stores by 1989, and eventually grew to more than 30,000 stores globally.

title: Launched Bean Stock options for all eligible employees including part-timers
statement: A year after Starbucks' first profit in 1990, Schultz introduced Bean Stock, a stock option plan enrolling 700 people from about 100 stores in the United States and Canada and making Starbucks the first privately owned U.S. company to offer stock options to all eligible employees, even part-timers.
outcome: Bean Stock remained a permanent component of the benefits package, anchoring the partner identity that distinguished Starbucks employment through the IPO era and beyond.

title: Took Starbucks public on Nasdaq
statement: Schultz completed Starbucks' initial public offering with 140 outlets, $73.5 million in revenue, and a market value of $271 million, selling roughly a 12% stake that raised about $25 million.
outcome: The proceeds financed a doubling of the store count within two years and gave Bean Stock grants a public market price, funding the national expansion.

title: Stepped down as CEO to become chief global strategist
statement: Schultz handed the chief executive role to former CFO Orin Smith and moved into the chief global strategist position to drive international expansion, remaining chairman while coordinating the first China store opening in January 1999.
outcome: The following years saw plans for one to two store openings per day in mainland China, but also domestic erosion, with the stock falling 75% from 2006 to 2008 as growth became dependent on new stores.

title: Returned as CEO and executed the Transformation Agenda
statement: Eight years after stepping down, Schultz reassumed the CEO role during the financial crisis and launched the Transformation Agenda: closing 7,100 U.S. stores for an afternoon of barista retraining on February 26, 2008, then shuttering 600 stores, eliminating 12,000 positions, rebuilding the management team, and doubling down on ethical sourcing and new technology.
outcome: From February 2008 to January 2009 the company cut an estimated 18,400 U.S. jobs and closed 977 stores worldwide, and the stock ultimately returned roughly sixteen-fold from the turnaround era.

title: Closed 8,000 stores for racial-bias training after the Philadelphia arrests
statement: After the April 12, 2018 arrests of two Black men at a Philadelphia store, Starbucks, with Schultz as executive chairman, closed about 8,000 U.S. stores for an afternoon of racial-bias education reaching 175,000 employees; Schultz personally apologized to the two men, and the company settled with them, including tuition support to finish their degrees.
outcome: The company reported no sales decline on its April 26 earnings call, with 2% same-store growth, and the closures became a benchmark case in corporate crisis response.

title: Suspended the stock buyback program upon returning as interim CEO
statement: In his first act as interim chief executive, Schultz suspended Starbucks' stock repurchasing program, reversing a plan announced the previous October to spend $20 billion on dividends and buybacks over three years, so the company could invest more in its people and stores.
outcome: The interim stint, dominated by the unionization fight, ended March 20, 2023, with Laxman Narasimhan taking over as chief executive, and Schultz testified before the Senate HELP committee days later.
